hello.title: Hello, Zig
hello.summary: Write your first Zig program, print text and numbers with std.debug.print, and run it with zig run.
hello.lesson.0: A program is a list of instructions for the computer. Zig is a fast language that turns your code into a program before it runs: this step is called **compiling**. This course uses **Zig 0.17**. Here is a complete Zig program:
hello.lesson.2: The first line loads the **standard library**, a collection of ready-made tools, and gives it the name `std`. `pub fn main() void` defines the function `main`: `fn` starts a function, `pub` makes it visible from outside the file, and `void` means it gives back no value. The program starts in `main` and runs the lines between `{` and `}` from top to bottom.
hello.lesson.3: `std.debug.print` shows text. It takes two things: the text in double quotes and a list of values in `.{}`. Here the list is empty. `\n` is a **new line**: `print` does not add one by itself. Every instruction ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.6: Inside the text, `{s}` and `{d}` are **placeholders**. Zig replaces them with the values from the list, in order. Use `{s}` for text (a **string**) and `{d}` for a number. Separate the values with commas: `.{ "Ada", 36 }`.
hello.lesson.8: The number of placeholders must match the number of values. If they do not match, or `{d}` gets a string, Zig stops with an error before the program runs. These checks catch many mistakes early.
hello.lesson.10: Save the code in a file that ends with `.zig`, for example `hello.zig`. In a terminal, the command `zig run hello.zig` compiles the file and runs the program right away.
hello.lesson.11: `std.debug.print` writes to the **standard error** stream (stderr), not to the normal output (stdout). In the terminal you see both, so it is perfect for learning. In the exercises, short examples show only the lines inside `main`.
hello.card.1: `pub fn main() void { }` is where the program starts
hello.card.4: `zig run hello.zig` compiles and runs a file
hello-1.prompt: Which line prints `Hi` and a new line?
hello-1.explain: `std.debug.print` needs the text in double quotes and a list of values in `.{}`, even when the list is empty.
hello-2.explain: The three `{d}` placeholders are replaced by `2`, `3` and the result of `2 + 3`, in this order.
hello-3.explain: The first text has no `\n`, so `B` is printed on the same line, right after `A`.
hello-4.statement: The command `zig run hello.zig` compiles the file and then runs the program.
hello-4.explain: `zig run` does both steps: it compiles the code and starts the program.
hello-5.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `Hello, Zig!`.
hello-5.explain: `{s}` is the placeholder for a string. `{d}` is for numbers.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the line that loads the standard library.
hello-6.explain: `const` gives the standard library the fixed name `std`.
hello-7.prompt: Build the first line of the `main` function.
hello-7.explain: `pub fn main() void {` defines the public function `main` that gives back no value.
hello-8.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints One, Two and Three.
hello-8.explain: The function starts with `pub fn main() void {` and ends with `}`. Between them, the lines run from top to bottom.
hello-9.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.explain: The instruction has no semicolon at the end. Write `std.debug.print("Hi\n", .{});`.
hello-11.explain: `42` is a number, so the placeholder must be `{d}`, not `{s}`.
hello-12.explain: Each placeholder takes the next value from the list: `{s}` gets `"Ada"` and `{d}` gets `36`.
variables.title: const, var and types
variables.summary: Store values with const and var, meet the types i32, u8, f64 and bool, and see why overflow is an error.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. In Zig you create one with `const` or `var`. A `const` value never changes. A `var` value can change later. Use `const` whenever you can.
variables.lesson.2: `var age: i32 = 36` creates a variable `age` of the **type** `i32` with the value `36`. The type comes after the colon `:`. `age += 1` adds 1 to `age`. You can also write `age = age + 1`.
variables.lesson.4: The type says what kind of value a variable holds. `i32` is a whole number that can be negative. `u8` is a whole number from 0 to 255 (`u` means **unsigned**: no minus sign). `f64` is a decimal number. `bool` is `true` or `false`. Print a `bool` with the placeholder `{}`.
variables.lesson.6: With `const name = "Ada"` you do not write a type: Zig works it out from the value. This is called **type inference**. A `var` needs a type when you give it a plain number, as in `var age: i32 = 36`.
variables.lesson.8: You calculate with `+`, `-` and `*`. `%` gives the rest of a division: 26 divided by 7 is 3, rest 5. `-=` and `*=` work like `+=`.
variables.lesson.9: Zig is strict: an unused variable is an error, and so is a `var` that never changes. The compiler then tells you to use `const`.
variables.lesson.11: Every whole-number type has a range. A `u8` holds 0 to 255. `const x: u8 = 256;` does not compile. If a value grows too big while the program runs, the program stops with the message `integer overflow` instead of giving a wrong result.
variables.lesson.13: Here `level` reaches 255, the largest `u8`. With `level += 6` the program would stop with `integer overflow`.
variables.card.0: `const x = 5;` never changes, `var y: i32 = 5;` can
variables.card.4: A value that does not fit its type is an error
variables-1.explain: `n` starts at 4, `+= 3` makes it 7, and `* 2` makes it 14.
variables-2.prompt: Which type can store the value `-3`?
variables-2.explain: `i32` is signed, so it can be negative. `u8` and `u32` are unsigned: they start at 0.
variables-3.explain: `limit` is a `const`, so you cannot give it a new value. Use `var limit: i32 = 10;` if it must change.
variables-4.explain: A `u8` holds only the numbers from 0 to 255.
variables-5.prompt: Complete the code so it compiles and prints `1`.
variables-5.explain: `count` changes, so it must be a `var`.
variables-6.prompt: Pick the right type for a price with cents.
variables-6.explain: `4.5` is a decimal number, so it needs a float type like `f64`.
variables-7.explain: 200 + 50 is 250, which still fits into a `u8`.
variables-8.prompt: Create a variable `score` of type `u32` that starts at 0 and can change.
variables-8.explain: `var` makes the value changeable, and the type `u32` comes after the colon.
variables-9.prompt: Match the type with the values it holds.
variables-10.explain: `lives` never changes, and Zig does not accept a `var` that is never changed. Write `const lives: u8 = 3;`.
variables-11.explain: A `var` that starts with a plain number needs a type. Write `var count: i32 = 0;`.
variables-12.explain: 260 does not fit into a `u8`, which ends at 255. Zig stops the program instead of printing a wrong number.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program decide with if and else, combine conditions with and and or, and pick a case with switch.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a **condition** is true. The condition goes in parentheses and must be a `bool`. The code after `else` runs when the condition is false.
conditions.lesson.2: You compare values with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`. Each comparison gives `true` or `false`. With `else if` you check another condition when the first one is false.
conditions.lesson.5: In Zig, `if` can also produce a value. `if (a) x else y` gives `x` when `a` is true and `y` otherwise. Here you need no braces.
conditions.lesson.8: Zig combines conditions with words: `a and b` is true when both are true, `a or b` when at least one is true. `!a` turns `true` into `false` and back.
conditions.lesson.11: `switch` compares one value with several cases. Each case has the form `value => result`. You can list several values with commas or a range like `3...5` (three dots, both ends included). A `switch` must cover every possible value, so you usually end with `else`.
conditions.lesson.13: Like `if`, `switch` gives a value. That is why the whole `switch` ends with `};`.
conditions-1.explain: 7 is greater than 5, so the first block runs.
conditions-2.explain: 10 divided by 3 leaves a rest of 1, so the condition is false and `kind` is `"B"`.
conditions-3.explain: `!b` is `true`, and `a` is `true`, so `a and !b` is `true`.
conditions-4.statement: In Zig, you write `&&` for a logical and.
conditions-4.explain: Zig uses the word `and`. `&&` is a compile error.
conditions-5.prompt: Complete the condition: the person must be 18 or older and have a ticket.
conditions-5.explain: Both parts must be true, so you need `and`.
conditions-6.prompt: Complete the `switch` so it covers all other numbers.
conditions-6.explain: `else` covers every value that no other case matches.
conditions-7.explain: `4...6` includes 4, so the second case matches.
conditions-8.prompt: Store `"minus"` in `sign` when `n` is below 0, otherwise `"plus"`.
conditions-8.explain: `if (condition) a else b` gives a value, which you can store directly in a constant.
conditions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order: a score of 90 or more prints A, 70 or more prints B, everything else prints C.
conditions-9.explain: Check the highest limit first. `else if` only runs when the first condition is false, and `else` catches the rest.
conditions-10.prompt: Match the operator with its meaning.
conditions-11.explain: `=` gives a new value. To compare, write `==`: `if (x == 5) {`.
conditions-12.explain: In Zig the condition of an `if` must be in parentheses: `if (n > 3) {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with while and for, count over ranges like 0..5, go through lists, and use break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A **loop** repeats code. `while` repeats as long as its condition is true. The counter must be a `var`, because it changes in every round.
loops.lesson.2: You can put the step into the loop head: `while (i < 5) : (i += 1)`. The part after the colon runs at the end of every round.
loops.lesson.4: If the condition of a `while` never becomes false, the loop runs forever. Make sure the counter changes.
loops.lesson.6: `for (0..3) |i|` runs once for each number from 0 up to 3, **without** 3: 0, 1 and 2. The name between the bars `|i|` holds the current number. Its type is `usize`, an unsigned whole number.
loops.lesson.8: `for` also goes through a list of values. `[_]u32{ 3, 5, 8 }` is such a list, called an **array**. You learn more about arrays in a later unit. `for (prices) |p|` gives you each value in turn.
loops.lesson.11: `continue` skips the rest of the current round and goes to the next one. `break` ends the loop at once.
loops.lesson.13: When an `if` controls only one instruction, you can write it on one line without braces, as in `if (i > 7) break;`.
loops.card.3: `break` ends the loop, `continue` skips to the next round
loops-1.explain: The loop adds 0, 1, 2 and 3. Together that is 6.
loops-2.explain: `0..3` gives 0, 1 and 2. There is no `\n` inside the loop, so they stay on one line.
loops-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
loops-3.explain: `2..5` gives 2, 3 and 4. The end, 5, is not included.
loops-4.explain: The end of a range is not included: `0..5` gives 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4.
loops-5.prompt: Complete the loop so it prints every item.
loops-5.explain: The name of the current value goes between two bars: `|item|`.
loops-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints 1, 2, 4 and 5.
loops-6.explain: `continue` skips only the round with 3. `break` would end the whole loop.
loops-7.explain: `n` becomes 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. 32 is the first value above 20, so the loop stops there.
loops-8.prompt: Build a loop head that runs while `i` is below 10 and adds 1 to `i` after every round.
loops-8.explain: The condition comes first in parentheses. The step follows after the colon.
loops-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program adds 1, 2 and 3 and prints `6`.
loops-9.explain: Create `total` first, add every number inside the loop, and print the result after the loop.
loops-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-10.pairs.0: repeats while a condition is true
loops-10.pairs.1: goes through a range or a list
loops-11.explain: The counter changes in every round, so it must be a `var`: `var i: u32 = 0;`.
loops-12.explain: `continue` skips every number that is not divisible by 3. From 1 to 9, only 3, 6 and 9 are left.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with parameters and return types, use their results, and solve problems with recursion.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** gives a piece of code a name, so you can use it many times. You already know `main`. You define your own functions with `fn`, outside of `main`, and call them by name.
functions.lesson.2: `name: []const u8` is a **parameter**: a name and its type. `[]const u8` is the type for text; a later unit explains it. The type after the parentheses is the **return type**. `void` means the function gives back nothing.
functions.lesson.3: To give back a value, write its type after the parentheses and use `return`. Separate several parameters with commas.
functions.lesson.5: Parameters are constants: you cannot change them inside the function. Zig also refuses unused parameters, and a result you do not use. To throw a result away on purpose, write `_ = add(1, 2);`.
functions.lesson.7: `return` ends the function at once. That is why `max` needs no `else`. A function can return any type, for example a `bool`.
functions.lesson.9: A function can call itself. This is called **recursion**. It needs a **base case** that stops the calls, otherwise they never end. The factorial of 4 is 4 * 3 * 2 * 1.
functions.lesson.11: The order of functions in a file does not matter. You can write `factorial` below `main` and still call it.
functions.card.0: `fn add(a: i32, b: i32) i32 { return a + b; }`
functions.card.2: Parameters are constants and must be used
functions.card.4: Recursion: a function calls itself, with a base case
functions-3.prompt: Which line correctly starts a function that takes two `i32` values and returns an `i32`?
functions-3.explain: Every parameter has its own type after a colon, and the return type follows the parentheses without a colon.
functions-4.explain: Parameters are constants, so `n = n / 2` is an error. Write `return n / 2;` instead.
functions-5.statement: You can call `add(1, 2);` on its own line and ignore the `i32` it returns.
functions-5.explain: Zig does not let you ignore a result by accident. Use it, or write `_ = add(1, 2);`.
functions-6.explain: `n % 2 == 0` is a comparison, so its result is `true` or `false`: a `bool`.
functions-7.explain: In Zig every function starts with the keyword `fn`.
functions-8.prompt: Build the first line of a function `square` that takes an `i32` named `x` and returns an `i32`.
functions-8.explain: `fn` comes first, then the name with its parameters, then the return type.
functions-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so `fact` computes the factorial.
functions-9.explain: The base case comes first. Otherwise the function would call itself before it can stop.
functions-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
functions-10.pairs.1: gives a value back to the caller
functions-11.explain: The function returns a number, so its return type must be `i32`, not `void`.
functions-12.explain: `add` has two parameters, so you must pass two values, for example `add(2, 3)`.
arrays.title: Arrays and slices
arrays.summary: Keep many values in arrays, look at parts of them with slices, and work with text as []const u8.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** holds a fixed number of values of the same type. `[3]i32` is an array of three `i32` values. With `[_]` Zig counts the values for you. You read a value by its **index** in square brackets. The first index is 0. `.len` gives the number of values.
arrays.lesson.2: In a `var` array you can change the values. The length stays the same.
arrays.lesson.4: An index must be smaller than `.len`. `nums[3]` on an array with three values is an error: the program does not compile, or it stops with `index out of bounds`.
arrays.lesson.6: A **slice** is a view of a part of an array. `nums[1..3]` contains the values at index 1 and 2: like a range, the end is not included. A slice also has `.len`. A function that takes a slice such as `[]const u32` works with arrays of any length. You pass a whole array with `&prices`.
arrays.lesson.9: Text is a list of bytes. A string is usually a slice of `u8`: `[]const u8`. Each byte is a number. `'h'` in single quotes is one character, which is also a `u8`. Print a whole string with `{s}` and one character with `{c}`. You cannot compare two strings with `==`: use `std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)`, which is `true` when both have the same bytes.
arrays.lesson.12: `for (names, 0..) |name, i|` goes through the array and counts at the same time: `name` is the value and `i` its index. `[_][]const u8` is an array of strings.
arrays.card.2: Text is `[]const u8`; compare with `std.mem.eql(u8, x, y)`
arrays-1.explain: Index 1 is 10 and index 3 is 20, because counting starts at 0.
arrays-2.explain: `s[1..4]` contains the bytes at index 1, 2 and 3: `e`, `l` and `l`.
arrays-3.prompt: What is the index of the first value in an array?
arrays-3.explain: Indexes start at 0, so `a[0]` is the first value.
arrays-5.statement: You compare two `[]const u8` strings with `==`.
arrays-5.explain: `==` does not work for slices. Use `std.mem.eql(u8, a, b)`.
arrays-6.prompt: Complete the code so it prints the number of values.
arrays-6.explain: `.len` is a field, not a function, so it has no parentheses.
arrays-7.prompt: Complete the parameter type so the function accepts a list of `u32` of any length.
arrays-7.explain: `[]const u32` is a slice. It works with arrays of any length.
arrays-8.prompt: Create an array `nums` with the values 1, 2 and 3.
arrays-8.explain: `[_]i32{ ... }` creates an array of `i32`. Zig counts the values for you.
arrays-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so the program prints `0: Ann` and `1: Bo`.
arrays-9.explain: Create the array first. The loop then gives each name together with its index.
arrays-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays-10.pairs.0: an array of three i32 values
arrays-11.prompt: The program should print the last value. Which line has the bug?
arrays-11.explain: The array has three values, so the last index is 2. Write `a[2]`.
arrays-12.explain: The program changes a value, so the array must be a `var`: `var scores = [_]u32{ 1, 2 };`.
structs.title: Structs
structs.summary: Group values into your own types with struct, give fields default values, and add methods that use self.
structs.lesson.0: A **struct** groups several values into one new type. Each value is a **field** with a name and a type. You create a value with `Point{ .x = 3, .y = 4 }` and read a field with a dot: `p.x`.
structs.lesson.2: Struct names start with a capital letter, like `Point`. In a `var` you can change the fields.
structs.lesson.5: A field can have a **default value**: `level: u32 = 1`. When you create the struct, you can leave this field out. All other fields must be set.
structs.lesson.8: A function inside a struct is a **method**. Its first parameter, usually called `self`, is the value you call it on. You write `r.area()`, and Zig passes `r` as `self`.
structs.lesson.10: `self` is a constant. To change fields, the method takes `self: *Counter`. The star `*` makes it a **pointer**: the method works on the original value. You can call such a method only on a `var`.
structs.lesson.12: Now you know what `.{ name, age }` in `std.debug.print` is: a struct without a type name that holds the values in order.
structs.card.0: `const Point = struct { x: i32, y: i32 };`
structs.card.3: `fn area(self: Rect) u32` is a method: `r.area()`
structs-1.prompt: `Point` has the fields `x` and `y`. What does this print?
structs-2.explain: `width` keeps its default value 80, and `height` is set to 50. Together that is 130.
structs-3.explain: `b.edges()` calls the method with `b` as `self`, so it returns 4 * 4.
structs-4.statement: When you create a struct, you can leave out a field that has a default value.
structs-4.explain: The field then gets its default value. Fields without a default must be set.
structs-5.explain: `self: Counter` is a constant. To change a field, the method needs `self: *Counter`.
structs-6.prompt: Complete the code that creates a `Point`.
structs-6.explain: When you create a struct, each field name starts with a dot: `.x = 1`.
structs-7.prompt: Complete the method so it can change `size`.
structs-7.explain: With `*Plant` the method gets a pointer to the original value and can change its fields.
structs-8.prompt: `Rect` has the fields `w` and `h`. Create a `Rect` named `r` with `w` 2 and `h` 3.
structs-8.explain: Write the type name, then the fields with a dot in front: `Rect{ .w = 2, .h = 3 }`.
structs-9.prompt: `Player` has a field `score` that starts at 0. Put the lines in order so the program prints `20`.
structs-9.explain: First add 10, then double it: (0 + 10) * 2 = 20. The other way round you get 10.
structs-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
structs-10.pairs.0: defines a new type with fields
structs-10.pairs.3: the value a method is called on
structs-10.pairs.4: a pointer to change the original
structs-11.explain: `increment` changes the counter, so `c` must be a `var`: `var c = Counter{};`.
structs-12.explain: Inside a method you reach the fields through `self`: `return self.w * self.h;`.
errors.title: Errors and optionals
errors.summary: Handle things that can fail with error sets, !T, try and catch, and values that can be missing with ?T and orelse.
errors.lesson.0: Some operations can fail. In Zig an **error** is a value. An **error set** lists the possible errors: `error{ Negative, TooOld }`. A function that can fail has a return type like `AgeError!i32`: the result is an `i32` **or** an error. `return AgeError.TooOld;` returns an error.
errors.lesson.2: You cannot use the result directly: you must handle the error first. `catch 0` means: use `0` if there is an error. With `catch |err|` you get the error itself and can react to it. `{}` prints an error.
errors.lesson.4: Here the return type is only `!u32`, and the error is written as `error.Odd`. Zig then collects the error set by itself. The `return` inside the `catch` block ends `main`.
errors.lesson.6: `try` is a short form: `try half(8)` gives the value, or returns the error to the caller at once. A function that uses `try` must have a `!` in its return type. Also `main` can be `pub fn main() !void`. If an error leaves `main`, the program stops and shows the error.
errors.lesson.9: Sometimes a value is missing. The type `?usize` is a `usize` **or** `null`, which means no value. `orelse` gives a fallback value for `null`.
errors.lesson.11: `if (opt) |v|` runs the block only when there is a value, and `v` holds it. The `else` block runs for `null`.
errors.lesson.13: Use `catch` for errors and `orelse` for optionals. An error tells you **why** something failed. `null` only says that there is no value.
errors.card.0: `const E = error{ A, B };` and `fn f() E!u32`
errors.card.1: `!u32` is a `u32` or an error; `try` passes the error on
errors-1.explain: `half(10)` returns 5. `half(7)` returns an error, so `catch` uses 0.
errors-2.explain: `x` is `null`, so it becomes 1. `y` has the value 7. 1 + 7 is 8.
errors-3.prompt: Which return type means "a `u32` or an error"?
errors-3.explain: `!` before the type means the function can return an error. `?` means the value can be `null`.
errors-5.statement: You can use `try` inside `pub fn main() void`.
errors-5.explain: `try` can return an error, so the function needs a `!` in its return type: `pub fn main() !void`.
errors-6.statement: A variable of type `u32` can hold `null`.
errors-6.explain: Only an optional type such as `?u32` can be `null`.
errors-7.prompt: `findPort()` returns a `?u16`. Complete the code so it uses 8080 when there is no port.
errors-7.explain: `orelse` gives a fallback value when an optional is `null`. `catch` is for errors.
errors-8.prompt: Complete the code so an error from `readCount()` is passed on to the caller.
errors-8.explain: `try` gives the value, or returns the error from `total` at once.
errors-9.prompt: Call `checkAge(input)` and store the result in `age`, or 0 if there is an error.
errors-9.explain: `catch 0` replaces an error with the value 0.
errors-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so `safeDiv` returns an error when `b` is 0.
errors-10.explain: The check must come before the division. After a `return`, no more code runs.
errors-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
errors-11.pairs.2: passes an error on to the caller
errors-11.pairs.3: uses 0 if there is an error
errors-11.pairs.4: uses 0 if the value is null
errors-12.explain: The function can return an error, so the return type needs a `!`: `fn check(n: u32) !u32 {`.
